item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Computational immunogenicity prediction for mRNA vaccines: benchmarks, bottlenecks, and the peptide-nucleotide gap
item.description: Abstract Computational prediction of T-cell epitopes has become indispensable to vaccine design, yet the field still relies on the assumption that how much of a given antigen is produced is fixed by its coding sequence. However, this is not the case with mRNA vaccines, i.e. the design of the mRNA template can vastly alter the quantity of the same protein produced. Codon usage, guanine-cytosine (GC) content, untranslated-region (UTR) design, and predicted secondary structure together define how fast the message is translated and how long it survives, and therefore how much antigen ever reaches the presentation pathway. This is a variable that no current immunogenicity predictor represents. Herein we appraise three decades of computational immunogenicity prediction, tracing the path from position-specific scoring matrices through pan-specific neural networks to transformer-based protein language models, and we use that history to expose the peptide-nucleotide gap between these tools and the way mRNA vaccines are designed. A structured synthesis of published evaluations of leading predictors across human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles, peptide lengths and data types shows that headline accuracy masks persistent deficiencies in predicting major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II, which underpins durable T-cell help, and rare alleles, which disproportionately affect under-represented populations. Four bottlenecks continue to constrain the field: class II prediction, T-cell receptor (TCR) recognition, immunodominance, and the disconnection between nucleotide-level design and peptide-level prediction. We argue that the last of these, which has drawn the least attention, is, in our assessment, the most likely to yield near-term gains for personalised cancer vaccines and pandemic preparedness, and we set out an architecture that couples translation-rate prediction to peptide presentation. Building it will require data that do not yet exist; we specify what must be measured, and on which platforms.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: G4SAINT enables interpretable prediction of RNA G-quadruplex binding proteins across the human proteome via domain-guided learning
item.description: Abstract RNA G-quadruplexes (RG4s) are noncanonical four-stranded RNA structures that regulate post-transcriptional processes and are linked to multiple diseases, yet identifying their binding proteins remains experimentally challenging and computationally limited. Here, we present G4SAINT, a deep learning framework that predicts RG4-binding potential directly from protein sequence, structural, and domain-guided features. G4SAINT integrates residue-level embeddings from protein language models with graph neural networks and domain-guided attention to capture complementary signals across modalities. Across multiple benchmarks, G4SAINT outperforms existing approaches and accurately highlights regions associated with RG4 recognition. By leveraging multi-task learning across related binding prediction tasks, it enables scalable application to large, uncharacterized human proteomes. Overall, G4SAINT provides a robust and extensible approach for systematic discovery of RG4-binding proteins, offering new opportunities for understanding RNA–protein interactions and identifying potential therapeutic targets. Our code and datasets are available at: https://github.com/o-nwn-o/G4SAINT .

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: ANCHOR: AI-NGS consensus hierarchy for optimized refinement of high-affinity binders from affinity maturation
item.description: Abstract Affinity maturation for the systematic discovery of high-affinity protein reagents remains a major challenge in display-based protein engineering, largely because phenotypic enrichment frequently fails to correlate with true binding affinity. To improve candidate identification, we developed ANCHOR, an artificial intelligence (AI) and next-generation sequencing (NGS) consensus hierarchy for optimized refinement that implements a score-decoupled, two-stage strategy. Enrichment-trained classifier and regression models are used to construct a candidate pool, from which group-specific consensus sequences are subsequently derived without ranking candidates solely by individual model scores. Using the phosphotyrosine-binding Fyn SH2 domain as a model system, the two models achieved strong performance on untouched independent test sets (classification area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) = 0.974; regression Pearson’s r = 0.870). By leveraging a biopanning-guided filter, ANCHOR reduced the searchable sequence space by approximately four orders of magnitude while maintaining a ~90% overlap with exhaustive screening and retained 297 enrichment-predicted variants. These variants were grouped by residue identity at the least-conserved position (P4) and consensus sequences were derived within each group. Among the 16 evaluable consensus variants, 9 (56%) matched or exceeded the affinity of TrM, a previously established 100-fold-improved superbinder, with several showing a two-fold further improvement. Exploratory analyses using a structural proxy indicated robustness to parameter choices and a higher observed hit rate for ANCHOR than for the evaluated alternatives. Application to a public anti-HER2 scFv yeast-display NGS dataset demonstrated computational portability across datasets and library designs. Collectively, ANCHOR provides a practical framework for prioritizing affinity-maturation candidates from display-derived NGS data.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Rethinking long-read haplotype phasing evaluation with Phasing F1-score
item.description: Abstract Haplotype phasing is central to genomic analysis and molecular diagnosis because whether variants occur in cis or in trans can strongly influence their functional and clinical consequences. Although long-read sequencing has substantially improved haplotype phasing, evaluation of long-read phasing algorithms still relies on conventional metrics, including switch error rate, Hamming error rate, block NG50 and phase percentage. Here we show that these metrics have fundamental limitations: they lack direct biological or clinical interpretability, can yield ambiguous rankings, and can even be artificially optimized by methods that produce biologically uninformative results. To address these limitations, we introduce Phasing F1-score, a single interpretable metric that quantifies how accurately and completely a method recovers pairwise phase relationships between heterozygous variants, which is relevant to identifying compound heterozygosity. Phasing F1-score integrates multiple aspects of performance, including phasing accuracy, contiguity and completeness, into a single measure, enables unambiguous comparison of phasing algorithms and is robust against artificial manipulation. We further developed PIE, a parallel toolkit for efficient computation of Phasing F1-score and region-specific phasing evaluation, and used it to benchmark major long-read phasing algorithms across 38 datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio HiFi platforms. Our results show that phasing performance varies across genomic regions, highlighting the need for region-specific method selection. To support practical applications, we developed PieStore, a database for querying region-specific phasing performance and selecting the most suitable phasing algorithm. Together, this work establishes Phasing F1-score as a robust and interpretable framework for haplotype phasing evaluation and provides PieStore as a practical resource.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: CausalMut: a causal deep learning framework for enzyme mutational effect prediction
item.description: Abstract Accurate prediction of enzyme mutational effects on catalytic kinetics is fundamental to data-driven enzyme engineering, yet existing deep learning models are fundamentally constrained by biases inherent in the data generation process. Experimental datasets are conditioned on prevailing experimental choices rather than uniform mutation interventions, which introduces spurious correlations that compromise model generalization. To address this challenge, CausalMut is proposed as a causality-guided deep learning framework that disentangles genuine mutational causal effects from confounding biases. The data generation mechanism is first formalized via a structural causal graph, revealing the experimental environment as a confounder that induces distributional imbalance across mutation types. Building on this analysis, CausalMut integrates two components: a Multi-scale Interaction Enhanced Network (MIENet), which captures complex interactions among the wild-type enzyme, substrate, and mutant without 3D structural information; and a Joint Focal-IPS optimization strategy, which corrects distributional imbalances at both the amino-acid and mutant levels. Comprehensive experiments on three real-world enzyme kinetic datasets ($k_{\text{cat}}$, $K_{m}$, and $k_{\text{cat}}/K_{m}$) against five state-of-the-art baselines demonstrate average improvements of 16.24% in root mean square error and 22.19% in $R^{2}$. CausalMut maintains consistent superiority under three biologically motivated distribution-shift settings, and case studies further demonstrate its ability to identify high-activity variants within a fixed screening budget, validating its robustness and practical utility.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: CN-RNN: a deep learning framework for copy number variants detection with exome sequencing data
item.description: Abstract Copy number variations (CNVs) are major structural genomic variants that contribute to a wide range of human diseases. Accurate CNV detection from whole-exome sequencing (WES) data remains challenging because existing callers often exhibit high false-positive rates and limited sensitivity for short CNVs. Moreover, current deep learning approaches do not fully integrate the complementary information provided by local read-depth patterns and region-level genomic features. Here we present CN-RNN, a two-stage framework that combines high-sensitivity candidate generation with deep learning-based candidate classification. The framework integrates a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) branch, which captures local depth changes and contextual dependencies across neighboring exons, with a parallel multi-layer perceptron (MLP) branch that incorporates region-level features including GC content, mappability, and exon length. The model was trained using parent-offspring trios from the Autism Sequencing Consortium (ASC), with training labels constructed through Mendelian inheritance filtering. In internal validation and evaluation with two independent external datasets constructed using distinct reference sets, CN-RNN consistently outperformed existing WES-based CNV callers and deep learning methods. These results demonstrate that integrating sequential read-depth patterns with region-level genomic features improves the accuracy and generalizability of CNV detection from WES data. CN-RNN provides a scalable tool for CNV profiling in population and clinical sequencing studies and is available at https://github.com/FeifeiXiao-lab/CN-RNN .

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Transformer models in genomics: from sequence analysis to population genetics and biodiversity
item.description: Abstract Modern genomics and artificial intelligence converge at a breakthrough point with the emergence of transformer-based large language models for genomic analysis. This review examines how transformer-based models have advanced genomic sequence analysis through novel tokenization strategies, self-attention mechanisms, and pre-training/fine-tuning paradigms. Unlike prior broad surveys, we focus on three sub-areas of genomics where transformer architectures have had a substantive impact: sequence-level analysis, population-level genetics, including genetic imputation and genome-wide association analysis, and biodiversity research, while addressing challenges like genome-scale computational demands, training biases, and interpreting attention in biological contexts. Looking forward, we outline how emerging foundation models, multi-modal integration, and biologically informed attention mechanisms could transform our understanding of genome function, providing a roadmap for leveraging genome language models to decode genome complexity and advance functional and population-level genomics.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Correction of the cytosine deamination artifacts in FFPE-based sequencing experiments
item.description: Abstract Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues remain an essential resource for molecular studies, yet formalin-induced cytosine deamination introduces characteristic C > T/G > A artifacts that compromise the accuracy of next-generation sequencing analyses. Numerous computational methods and enzymatic DNA repair strategies have been proposed to reduce these artifacts, but no systematic comparison across tools and experimental conditions exists. Here, we evaluate the performance of seven computational approaches (SOBDetector, Ideafix, MicroSEC, FFPolish, DeepOmics FFPE/FFPE-PLUS, FFPErase) together with the NEBNext® FFPE DNA Repair Mix v2, a multi-enzyme repair system applied during DNA preparation. Using three independent datasets, one based on whole genome sequencing (CGCI-BL) and two on whole exome sequencing (TCGA-PC and SUT-LUAD, the latter containing enzymatically repaired samples), and matched fresh-frozen samples as the gold standard, we assess precision, sensitivity, and artifact reduction efficiency across all methods. We further examine the potential synergy between enzymatic repair and post-sequencing computational filtering. Our results provide practical guidelines for FFPE artifact correction and demonstrate that enzymatic treatment provides the best results, while among the computational methods, FFPErase offers the most robust reduction of cytosine deamination artifacts while maximizing the retention of true somatic variants.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Integration of single-cell multi-omic data with graph-based topic modelling
item.description: Abstract Recent advances in single-cell biology enable the profiling of multiple molecular layers, such as the transcriptome, epigenome, and surface proteins, within a single cell. Tackling the complexity of these data from multiple perspectives allows researchers to gain the most comprehensive insights into cellular biological properties. Here, we propose a graph-based topic modelling method called bionSBM. Our method leverages well-known community-detection methods for multipartite graphs and the interpretability of topic modelling to cluster and explain high-dimensional, sparse, and noisy single-cell matrices. We applied our algorithm to paired single-cell multi-omics data, such as 10X Multiome, SHARE-seq, and CITE-seq. We showed that it achieves superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods for ground-truth label retrieval, with high specificity and distinct biological interpretability.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Koinetic: a graph-based distance as a new ecological metric for microbial community differential analysis
item.description: Abstract Phylogeny-aware beta diversity measures are essential in microbiome research, yet widely used metrics such as UniFrac and its variants rely on independent branch-length contributions and do not satisfy the Euclidean property, leading to distortions in ordination and kernel-based tests. These limitations underscore the need for a distance that is both phylogenetically coherent and geometrically valid. We introduce the Koinos Kinetic Distance (Koinetic), a phylogeny-aware dissimilarity that views microbial communities as interconnected assemblies rather than isolated taxa. ”Koinos” emphasizes collective evaluation, while ”kinetic” reflects how differences propagate dynamically across ecological networks and phylogenetic lineages. Koinetic leverages a graph Laplacian–based kernel to weight community differences by shared phylogeny, capturing ecological connectivity and clade relatedness. This design ensures Euclidean validity and enables seamless integration with kernel-based methods as well as geometry-preserving ordination. Controlled simulations and analyses of eight microbiome datasets spanning diverse body sites, disease contexts, and microbial profiling modalities demonstrate Koinetic’s broad applicability. Compared with classical and phylogenetic metrics, including weighted, unweighted, and generalized UniFrac, unweighted Koinetic can improve power for phylogenetically localized prevalence shifts in the simulated settings, while weighted Koinetic performs comparably with weighted and generalized UniFrac under abundance-driven signals. Koinetic also shows strong performance in PERMANOVA and MiRKAT analyses assessing associations between microbial community composition and host phenotypes. Koinetic thus provides a general foundation for phylogeny-aware analysis, with a consistent geometric basis for visualization and statistical inference.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: ESGI: efficient splitting of generic indices in single-cell sequencing data
item.description: Abstract Single-cell sequencing technologies increasingly rely on complex nucleotide barcoding schemes to encode cellular identities, experimental conditions, and molecular modalities within a single experiment. While demultiplexing, alignment, and unique molecular identifier (UMI)-based quantification form the core preprocessing steps that transform raw sequencing reads into analyzable single-cell data, existing pipelines are often tightly coupled to specific experimental designs and typically assume fixed barcode positions and substitution-only error models. As a result, many assays employing combinatorial, variable-length, or multimodal barcoding designs require custom, hard-coded preprocessing solutions that are difficult to generalize and maintain. Here, we present efficient splitting of generic indices (ESGI), a flexible framework for demultiplexing and processing single-cell sequencing data with arbitrary barcode architectures. ESGI operates directly on raw FASTQ files using a generic barcode pattern specification, supports barcode matching with insertions and deletions via Levenshtein distance, accommodates variable-length barcodes, and provides detailed quality metrics for barcode assignment. ESGI optionally integrates genome alignment via STAR and performs feature quantification and UMI collapsing to generate cell-by-feature count matrices. ESGI is well documented and readily applicable to novel single-cell experiments. We demonstrate the versatility of ESGI across six datasets spanning four distinct single-cell technologies, including combinatorial indexing–based transcriptomic and multimodal assays, feature barcode-based protein measurements, and spatial barcoding data. Across these applications, ESGI robustly demultiplexes complex barcode designs that are not natively supported by existing pipelines, while producing results comparable with established workflows where applicable. ESGI provides a general solution for processing a wide range of barcoded single-cell sequencing data, enabling rapid adoption and analysis of emerging experimental designs.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Modeling distinct pathogenesis of early- and late-onset preeclampsia via hierarchical representation learning of interactome
item.description: Abstract Objectives: We developed and validated the pathogenesis models by hierarchical representation learning of interactomes connecting endometrial maturation, placentation, chorioamnionitis, and hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme, and low platelet (HELLP) syndrome. Methods: We utilized 19 gene sets from our previous work to infer interactomes to develop ( n = 177) and validate ( n = 352) explainable artificial intelligence models for each preeclampsia subtype using deep-insight visible neural network, gradient-weighted class activation mapping, and large language model. Results: The hierarchically learned representations identified novel genes for late-onset preeclampsia (LOPE), similar to chorioamnionitis ( ANKRD13A , SLA ), and HELLP syndrome ( PDE5A ). We also identified novel genes for early-onset preeclampsia (EOPE), similar to HELLP syndrome ( SWAP70 , GREM2 , GPR146 , PIP5K1B , EZR ). Conclusions: Our pathogenesis models connected HELLP syndrome with both LOPE and EOPE. However, chorioamnionitis was only connected with LOPE.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Interaction-finder: automated literature-based discovery of biological entity associations with quote-level provenance
item.description: Abstract Identifying interactions between biological entities is a cornerstone of molecular research, but assembling such lists from the literature is slow and tedious. For many research questions, no curated database exists, leaving researchers to survey the relevant literature themselves. We present interaction-finder, a tool that automates this process: given a topic string and user-defined entity types, it discovers relevant literature through LLM-guided iterative search, extracts candidate associations from full-text articles, and produces a ranked list where every association is backed by quoted passages verified against the source text. A self-contained interactive HTML report enables rapid triage of the results. Evaluated across 60 topics in three domains (celltype–cellmarker, disease–gene, and ligand–receptor), interaction-finder recovers up to 4.3× as many known associations as the best of single-shot prompting and an off-the-shelf deep-research framework, with all extracted quotes verified against source text. To assess candidates unrecognised from the gold-standard databases, we scored each candidate using an independent LLM judge blind to the tool’s reasoning. Across the three domains, unverified candidates score similarly to gold-standard associations. We find the gold-standard associations are enriched at the top of our ranked candidates, with an overall recall@20 of 0.61.Interaction-finder is freely available at https://github.com/tecosaur/interaction_finder under an MIT licence.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: ASAOT: an accentuated structure-differentiated asymmetric optimal transport model for cell type and single-cell spatial mapping
item.description: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics (STs) characterizes spatiotemporal gene expression and facilitates analysis of cellular architecture and cell–cell crosstalk within tissue microenvironments. However, existing spatial deconvolution methods employ globally fixed smoothing without local sharpening, which blurs cellular boundaries and impedes reconstruction of layered, heterogeneous cellular patterns in brain tissue. Here, we present Accentuated Structure-differentiated Asymmetric Optimal Transport (ASAOT), a deconvolution framework built on structure-enhanced asymmetric optimal transport. Coupled with spatial neighborhood constraints, ASAOT introduces a differentiated accentuated sharpening term to maintain global spatial continuity, enhance boundary detection, and preserve spot-level expression heterogeneity. Using asymmetric optimal transport, the framework jointly estimates spot-wise cell-type proportions and performs spatial assignment of reference single-cell coordinates. Benchmarks on diverse simulated datasets demonstrate that ASAOT achieves competitive overall accuracy and robustness across moderate spatial resolutions, with the best average comprehensive rank among tested methods. Applications to mouse olfactory bulb and cerebral cortex datasets demonstrate that ASAOT reduces signal diffusion and boundary distortion, effectively recovering layered brain anatomy and stratified cell distributions to build interpretable spatial maps of reference single-cell profiles. Collectively, ASAOT addresses critical drawbacks of conventional methods via a sharpening regularization term, serving as a reliable tool for STs analysis and mechanism exploration of tissue spatial organization.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: HGMetaADR: a multimodal heterogeneous graph meta-learning framework for generalized adverse drug reaction prediction
item.description: Abstract Early identification of adverse drug reactions (ADRs), which refer to harmful or unintended responses to medications taken at normal doses, is crucial for reducing clinical trial failures and associated economic costs. However, existing ADR datasets often exhibit a long-tailed label distribution and lack sufficient training examples for rare side effects, making it difficult for vanilla supervised learning models to generalize to underrepresented classes. To address these issues, we propose HGMetaADR, a novel heterogeneous graph-based meta-learning framework for ADR prediction. Built upon a multimodal biomedical knowledge graph, this approach integrates complementary drug-related data, including molecular structures, protein sequences, side effects, and therapeutic indications. It employs a hierarchical attention mechanism to capture semantic dependencies across heterogeneous entities and adopts a model-agnostic meta-learning strategy to enhance adaptation to small-sample classes. We evaluate HGMetaADR under three scenarios— few-shot , zero-shot , and majority —to simulate real-world conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HGMetaADR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, ablation studies and pathway enrichment analyses reveal the underlying biological mechanisms linking protein targets, therapeutic indications, and side effects, thereby validating the effectiveness of incorporating heterogeneous biomedical knowledge into ADR modeling.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Surrogate-guided self-play Monte Carlo tree search for antimicrobial peptide sequence optimization and in vitro antibacterial assessment
item.description: Abstract The rapid emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogens necessitates the development of novel therapeutic agents, yet the de novo design of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) is challenged by the vast combinatorial search space and the difficulty of balancing efficacy with toxicity. To address these limitations, we introduce a reinforcement learning framework that employs surrogate-guided self-play Monte Carlo tree search to explore the peptide landscape. By integrating surrogate models for predicted antimicrobial activity, HemoDL-predicted hemolytic propensity, and ESMFold structural confidence, the system performs multi-property computational optimization and candidate prioritization. In silico analysis demonstrated that the optimized peptides adopt amphipathic α-helical structures with high predicted folding confidence and possess favorable docking scores against Staphylococcus aureus resistance targets, including PBP2a and MurA. To assess the biological relevance of the computationally prioritized candidates, 16 peptides were synthesized and evaluated by agar dilution against a 37-strain bacterial panel over a concentration range of 0.25–64 μg/ml. AMP2, AMP7, and AMP9 achieved complete inhibition of at least one tested strain, corresponding to 3 of 16 synthesized candidates (18.75%). AMP12 and AMP13 showed partial growth reduction without complete inhibition within the tested range, whereas the remaining 11 candidates showed no complete inhibition. These findings quantify the current gap between surrogate-defined computational enrichment and assay-specific antibacterial activity. The strain-dependent experimental outcomes further indicate that surrogate, docking, and structural scores do not fully capture all determinants of antibacterial efficacy. The experimental assessment was limited to bacterial agar-dilution activity; mammalian-cell cytotoxicity, wet-lab hemolysis, and peptide-stability assays were not performed. In conclusion, this study establishes a computational framework for the design of bioactive peptides and provides structural insights for bridging the gap between deep learning predictions and experimental outcomes.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: GLAlign integrates single-cell multi-omics data via global manifold and local marker gene alignment
item.description: Abstract Integrating heterogeneous single-cell multi-omics datasets remains challenging because different modalities are measured in distinct feature spaces and lack cell level pairing. Existing manifold alignment or feature conversion framework are often affected by weak cross-modality associations, geometric ambiguity, and overcorrection. Here we present GLAlign (Global manifold and Local marker gene Alignment), an optimization framework that jointly leverages global manifold structure and local marker gene information to integrate single-cell multi-omics data. GLAlign learns a shared latent space through a global objective comprising maximum mean discrepancy, distortion, and penalty terms, together with a local contrastive triplet loss guided by cross-modality marker gene overlap between independently inferred clusters. We demonstrate GLAlign’s methodological contribution in extending the manifold alignment by biologically informed prior to ensure geometrically plausible and biologically correct alignments without requiring paired cells or manual cell type annotations. We evaluated GLAlign on simulated data and real datasets spanning PBMC scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq, mouse brain SNARE-seq, single-donor and multi-batch CITE-seq, and NCI-N87 scDNA-seq/scRNA-seq integration. Across the evaluated datasets, GLAlign achieved strong modality mixing and biological conservation, remained stable under moderate cell type imbalance and variations in clustering and marker information, and supported cross-modality label transfer and paired cell recovery. These results demonstrate that biologically structured coupling of global and local alignment provides an interpretable framework for heterogeneous single-cell multi-omics integration. GLAlign is freely available at https://github.com/Bateer-Bio/GLAlign .

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Biosemantic graph transfer learning for cross-patient cell type annotation and cell–cell interaction analysis in tumor single-cell RNA sequencing
item.description: Abstract The exploration of cellular heterogeneity within the tumor microenvironment (TME) via single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is essential for understanding cancer progression and response to therapy. Current scRNA-seq approaches, however, lack spatial context and rely on incomplete datasets of ligand–receptor interactions, limiting accurate cell type annotation and cell–cell communication inference. This study addresses these challenges using a novel graph neural network model that enhances cell-type prediction and cell-interaction analysis. Our study utilized a dataset consisting of 49 024 cells from 19 patients across three cancer types: leukemia, breast invasive carcinoma, and colorectal cancer. The proposed scGSL model demonstrated robust performance, achieving an average accuracy of 84.83%, precision of 86.23%, recall of 81.51%, and an F1 score of 80.92% across all datasets. These metrics represent a significant enhancement over existing methods, which typically exhibit lower performance metrics. Additionally, by reviewing existing literature on gene interactions within the TME, the scGSL model proves to robustly identify biologically meaningful gene interactions in an unsupervised manner, validated by significant expression differences in key gene pairs across various cancers. The source code and data used in this study can be found at https://github.com/LiYuechao1998/scGSL .

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Explainability in transformer-based models: methods, tools, and applications in natural language processing and bioinformatics
item.description: Abstract In recent years, Transformer-based models have become state of the art in natural language processing (NLP) and have achieved exceptional performance in a wide range of tasks. Their impact has extended to critical domains such as healthcare and bioinformatics. Transformer models are nonlinear and complex, making it challenging for researchers to understand different aspects of model performance and decision-making processes. Given the widespread use of these models in data processing, particularly in applications related to human health, the need for interpretable and transparent models has become essential. The goal of this paper is to provide a comprehensive review of explainability methods for transformer models, as well as the interpretability tools commonly used in NLP and bioinformatics. First, interpretable methods in different domains are broadly categorized. It then presents a focused discussion on strategies for explaining transformer-based models. By analyzing and comparing these methods, their strengths, applicability to transformers, and limitations are highlighted. As model complexity increases, understanding model behavior becomes more challenging. Explainability techniques can help address this gap and support tasks such as error diagnostics, model improvement, and other applications. Greater clarity in a model’s decision-making process can increase user confidence. Interpretable models are particularly important in critical applications such as drug design, where they can support deeper investigation and facilitate new discoveries. Finally, this paper outlines potential directions for future research.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: CRAFT: an antigen-specific TCR generative model for conditional de novo design with physicochemical constraints
item.description: Abstract T-cell receptors (TCRs) are essential to adaptive immunity and mediate the recognition and elimination of malignant or infected cells through antigen-specific interactions. Despite the clinical progress of TCR-based immunotherapies, computational de novo design of antigen-specific TCRs remains difficult. The main difficulties include the complexity of peptide–major histocompatibility complex (pMHC)-dependent recognition, strict physicochemical requirements at the binding interface, and the small amount of paired training data available for model development. Current generative approaches depend largely on 1D sequence statistics and do not capture pMHC presentation context, interfacial physicochemical properties, and native receptor priors within a unified framework. We present conditional reconstruction of antigen fragments for TCRs (CRAFT), a decoupled generative model for pMHC-conditioned de novo design of antigen-specific TCR CDR3$\beta $ sequences under physicochemical constraints. With large-scale pretraining, CRAFT learns base representations that help reduce the limitations imposed by data scarcity. We further incorporate antigen-derived contextual information to guide antigen-specific TCR CDR3$\beta $ sequence design. The architecture comprises an antigen encoder (PrimeBERT) that captures the pMHC context and an autoregressive decoder (PrimeTCR) that preserves native receptor priors. The encoder and decoder are coupled through cross-attention and augmented with Atchley factor embeddings, allowing CRAFT to incorporate physicochemical constraints relevant to antigen-conditioned receptor design during sequence decoding. Across multiple evaluations, CRAFT demonstrates competitive sequence naturalness, together with favorable performance in specific binding, and predicted structural plausibility. Overall, CRAFT provides a computational framework for developing personalized tumor immunotherapies. It also holds potential to support clinical translation by enabling the efficient, targeted discovery of candidate TCRs.
