item.title: Bioinformatics: SeekRBP: leveraging sequence–structure integration with reinforcement learning for receptor-binding protein identification
item.description: Abstract Motivation Receptor-binding proteins (RBPs) initiate viral infection and determine host specificity, serving as key targets for phage engineering and therapy. However, the identification of RBPs is complicated by their extreme sequence divergence, which often renders traditional homology-based alignment methods ineffective. While machine learning offers a promising alternative, such approaches struggle with severe class imbalance and the difficulty of selecting informative negative samples from heterogeneous tail proteins. Existing methods often fail to balance learning from these “hard negatives” while maintaining generalization. Results We present SeekRBP, a sequence–structure framework that models negative sampling as a sequential decision-making problem. By employing a multi-armed bandit strategy, SeekRBP dynamically prioritizes informative non-RBP sequences based on real-time training feedback, complemented by a multimodal fusion of protein language and structural embeddings. Benchmarking demonstrates that SeekRBP consistently outperforms static sampling strategies. Furthermore, a case study on Vibrio phages validates that SeekRBP effectively identifies RBPs to improve host prediction, highlighting its potential for large-scale annotation and synthetic biology applications. Availability and implementation The source code of SeekRBP is available via: https://github.com/Saillxl/SeekRBP .

item.title: Bioinformatics: DTBNet: multimodal 3D geometric perception with hierarchical attention for robust drug–target interaction and binding affinity prediction
item.description: Abstract Motivation Accurate prediction of drug–target interactions (DTIs) and binding affinity (DTA) constitutes a core challenge in accelerating drug discovery. While existing computational methods have made progress, most models struggle to capture critical physicochemical interactions in 3D space due to reliance on 1D sequences or 2D graph structures, and exhibit limited generalization in cold-start scenarios. This study proposes DTBNet, a unified prediction framework integrating multimodal geometric perception and hierarchical attention. The framework constructs heterogeneous embeddings combining local chemical details with global biological information by incorporating protein 3D geometric features and multilevel drug representations. During cross-modal interaction, atom–residue cross-attention first captures pair-specific local associations, followed by group-level multi-head self-attention that integrates complementary chemical-semantic, global structural, and local geometric interaction representations. Results Experiments on benchmark datasets (Davis, KIBA, and PDBBind) demonstrate that compared with the optimal baseline models, DTBNet achieves up to 19.8% reduction in mean squared error and 8.0% improvement in Pearson correlation coefficient, maintaining optimal performance in drug cold-start, target cold-start, and completely novel pairing scenarios, showcasing robust cross-domain adaptability. Independent validation on GPCR targets achieves RMSE 0.783, confirming real-world applicability. Visualization analyses reveal DTBNet precisely identifies interaction sites between key transmembrane helical domain residues and drug aromatic rings, with attention distribution highly consistent with experimentally resolved binding conformations. These results establish DTBNet as a new performance benchmark through 3D geometric perception and dynamic attention mechanisms, providing interpretable molecular insights for structure-based rational drug design and demonstrating broad potential in virtual screening and target discovery. Availability and implementation The source code and data are available at https://github.com/wyx2012/DTB_Net .

item.title: Nature Methods: Deciphering the gene-centric spatial dynamics across tissue and time with GeneSPOT
item.description: GeneSPOT is a framework that enables gene-centric exploration of spatial transcriptomic data.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: How far can you borrow? Divergence limits of cross-species Gene Ontology enrichment in non-model organisms
item.description: Abstract Functional interpretation of omics data from non-model species almost always relies on borrowing Gene Ontology (GO) annotations from a model organism—often a distant one ( Arabidopsis for plants, zebrafish or human for fish)—and running enrichment analysis on inferred orthologs. How far this practice can be pushed before the enrichment result degrades has never been quantified at the level practitioners use. We present the first systematic benchmark of the divergence-tolerance of cross-species GO-transfer enrichment, across six focal species spanning three eukaryotic kingdoms, each with 15–22 reference species tiling a continuous phylogenetic gradient. Set-level fidelity—measured as redundancy-robust Wang semantic similarity between transferred and experimental-truth enriched term sets—declines monotonically with distance, collapsing to chance at the clade boundary in some panels (fish, rice) while remaining well above it in others (insect, fungi, mammal) (half-collapse identity, ID50, ~40%–59%). At fixed distance, a richer reference raises recall but lowers precision, quantifying a long-recognized but unresolved trade-off. Conserved processes transfer reliably to distant references whereas taxon-specific processes do not, a pattern consistent across all six focal species tested. Whole-genome duplication degrades transfer only when ohnolog retention is high, showing up as sensitivity to the orthology method rather than a steeper decline. An independent, GO-free measure of expression conservation supports the curves in vertebrates. We condense these results into a focal-species × distance reliability guide and a step-by-step decision protocol that let researchers judge, before analysis, whether borrowed-GO enrichment can be trusted for their species and question.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Impact of training data on deep learning–based RNA 3D structure quality assessment
item.description: Abstract Accurate reference-free assessment of predicted RNA 3D structures is essential for large-scale RNA modeling, yet the impact of training data on deep learning–based quality predictors remains poorly understood. Here, we present a systematic cross-training analysis of three deep learning predictors for RNA 3D structure quality assessment, each originally developed on distinct training sets. By retraining each predictor on alternative (nonnative) datasets—including RNA3DQA, a new set created specifically for this project—and evaluating performance on independent RNA-Puzzles benchmarks, we systematically assess the relative contributions of model architecture and training data composition. Our results reveal pronounced differences in cross-dataset generalization, with predictors often performing better when trained on nonnative datasets than on their native ones. Notably, the impact of the training datasets varied across predictors, with RNA3DQA yielding the overall best accuracy and ranking stability results specifically for the ARES model. Native training sets yielded better performance for RNA3DCNN and lociPARSE. These findings demonstrate that the characteristics of the training data play a dominant, model-dependent role in shaping the performance and robustness of reference-free RNA 3D structure quality assessment methods. We conclude with practical recommendations for designing transferable training datasets and for benchmarking deep learning–based quality predictors in RNA structural bioinformatics.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: scYOU: a multi-scale yoked optimization and unsupervised framework for analysis of cellular heterogeneity and complex-associated protein module recovery
item.description: Abstract Advances in high-resolution proteomic technologies are enabling systematic characterization of cellular heterogeneity and protein functional programs at increasing depth. However, existing computational approaches typically focus on either cell-level organization or protein-level structure, lacking a unified framework that jointly models both entities. Here we present scYOU, a multi-scale yoked optimization and unsupervised framework that simultaneously captures cellular heterogeneity and protein functional organization through a dual-channel neural network architecture. scYOU learns cell and protein embeddings in parallel while coupling the two views through a supercell-constrained alignment strategy. Supercells are constructed based on high-order expression similarity and define grouping structures over cells. A dual-channel alignment objective is imposed at the reconstruction level, such that reconstructed expression profiles of cells within the same supercell are encouraged to converge, whereas those from different supercells remain separable. On the protein side, Gene Ontology–derived functional similarity priors regularize protein embeddings to preserve molecular biological consistency. Across diverse benchmark datasets, scYOU achieves strong and relatively consistent clustering performance together with improved embedding separability, while the learned protein representations support embedding-guided refinement of existing interaction networks and the recovery of complex-associated protein modules. These results establish scYOU as a structurally coupled, multi-level representation learning framework for proteomic data, and highlight the importance of jointly modeling cellular heterogeneity and protein functional modules within a unified computational paradigm. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/anchor-hue/scYou .

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Graphics processing unit-accelerated quantum simulation for molecular biology and drug discovery: algorithms, platforms, and emerging applications
item.description: Abstract Artificial intelligence has intensified the need for methods that describe molecular systems with quantum-mechanical accuracy. Gate-based quantum computing offers a principled framework for simulating electronic structure, molecular interactions, and biological processes at a fidelity inaccessible to classical force fields or density functional theory alone, yet scarce, noisy hardware limits direct experimentation. Graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated quantum simulation has emerged as a practical bridge, allowing quantum algorithms to be developed, validated, and benchmarked on classical infrastructure at 30–40 noiseless qubits, and far beyond where tensor-network methods apply. Unlike recent reviews organized around quantum machine learning (QML) or around hardware, this review is organized around the simulation layer itself and asks, for each domain, what can be established in simulation, what requires a quantum processor, and how the two connect in one hardware-agnostic workflow. We examine how the variational quantum eigensolver, quantum phase estimation, and sample-based hybrid schemes address electronic structure in small-molecule pharmacology; how quantum-enhanced conformational sampling complements AlphaFold; and how QML introduces alternative feature spaces for drug–target, structure–activity, and genomic modeling. We compile published GPU benchmarks, identify the molecular systems for which tensor-network simulation is and is not adequate, explain how GPU platforms accelerate error mitigation, and critically assess 2023–6 developments, including quantum-centric supercomputing, hybrid quantum Monte Carlo on trapped-ion hardware, protein binding-site prediction on utility-scale processors, below-threshold error correction, and a classically verifiable quantum-advantage claim. Framing GPU simulation as a near-term enabler rather than a final objective, the review offers a practical entry point for biological and pharmaceutical scientists.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: A recall-rescue fuzzy layer over paired Z-DNA Hunter scans for fast Z-DNA detection
item.description: Abstract Accurate detection of Z-DNA-forming regions is limited by the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity in sequence-based methods. We present Z-DNA-Fuzzy Hunter 1.1.0—a fast and interpretable protocol that extends Z-DNA Hunter through a dual-scan strategy combined with a fuzzy expert layer. A permissive scan (model 2, minimum length 6 bp, threshold 30%) captures a broad candidate set, while a stringent scan (model 2, minimum length 10 bp, threshold 60%) provides high-confidence support. These outputs are integrated using fuzzy inference incorporating sequence signal, cross-scan support, genomic context, and bias penalties. On the audited 385-locus Shin analysis, the protocol achieves balanced accuracy 0.883 (recall 0.862, specificity 0.904), comparable with the published Z-DNABERT operating point, while alternative modes increase specificity to 0.973. The paired scans are combined by a transparent, configurable prioritization layer with an adjustable recall–specificity trade-off. The local workflow requires only a FASTA (Fast-All sequence alignment format), sequence and transcription start site annotation. The tool is freely available at https://github.com/mifo123/zdna-fuzzy-hunter .

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: spaDWGCN: a spatial distance weighted graph convolution network for accurate spatial tissue structure identification
item.description: Abstract The continuous development of spatial transcriptomics enables us to obtain gene expression matrices alongside spatial coordinate labels for cells or spots, providing tools for understanding spatial tissue microenvironments and spatially resolved cell–cell interactions. Although numerous methods have been developed to identify spatial tissue architecture, most of them adopt binary adjacency matrices that treat all neighboring cells equally, and few comprehensively incorporate distance information into both graph construction and feature representation. Here we introduce spaDWGCN, a spatial distance weighted graph convolutional network algorithm that takes cellular gene expression and microenvironment composition as inputs. This approach introduces fine-grained distance weighting at two levels: replacing the conventional 0–1 binary adjacency matrix with a distance-weighted adjacency matrix at the graph level, and substituting the neighbor count matrix with a distance-weighted microenvironment composition matrix at the feature level. Furthermore, spaDWGCN jointly models gene expression and microenvironment composition through separate graph convolutional network branches and trainable fusion, integrating transcriptional patterns with their local neighborhood context within a unified framework. Experiments on spatial transcriptomics multi-platform datasets, including MERFISH, STARmap, Stereo-seq, Slide-seqV2, and 10× Visium, demonstrate that this distance-weighted strategy achieves competitive performance in spatial domain identification and other downstream analyses.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Structured multi-view relational learning for drug response prediction
item.description: Abstract Drug response prediction (DRP) requires models that jointly characterize molecular drug structure and heterogeneous cellular states. Although recent deep learning approaches have integrated multi-omics profiles with drug representations, many treat omics views as parallel feature sources or merge them before relational modeling, which can weaken omics-view-specific cell-line relation structures. Here, we propose MulDR, a structured multi-view relational learning framework that preserves omics-view-specific cell-line relation structures before drug-conditioned cell–drug interaction. MulDR constructs separate relation structures for pathway activity, gene expression, mutation, and DNA methylation, learns view-specific relational cell representations, and uses complementary motif-level, geometry-aware molecular graph, and Morgan fingerprint drug representations to condition their fusion. With this design, cell-line similarity remains view-dependent until the interaction stage, rather than being prematurely compressed into a single feature or relation space. Extensive experiments show that MulDR consistently outperforms representative and recent baselines under the same evaluation protocol, reducing root mean square error by 6.07% relative to the strongest baseline. Cold-start evaluations on unseen drugs and cell lines further show that MulDR generalizes to previously unseen entities, while ablation studies show that removing either view-specific relational modeling or drug-conditioned fusion consistently compromises predictive performance. Together, these results suggest that preserving omics-specific cell-line relations before drug-conditioned interaction modeling provides an effective strategy for robust DRP.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: CalDyn: an advanced high-throughput automated algorithm for monitoring intracellular calcium dynamics and electrophysiological signals in patient-derived cells
item.description: Abstract Background Quantitative analysis of intracellular calcium and electrophysiological signals is challenging when signals exhibit baseline drift, low-amplitude events, irregular waveforms, or multicomponent transients. We developed CalDyn, a MATLAB-based graphical application for automated peak detection, waveform characterization, event classification, batch processing, quality control and data export. Methods CalDyn combines Savitzky–Golay filtering, LOESS-assisted derivative detection, optional baseline correction, waveform-boundary fitting and rule-based peak classification. It was evaluated on calcium recordings (healthy and disease-associated hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, hiPSC-derived neurons, primary skeletal myotubes), current-clamp action potentials and cardiac optical-mapping signals. Outputs were compared with PeakInspector, Clampfit and BV Workbench using paired and Bland–Altman analyses. Detection was assessed against 142 expert-annotated events and synthetic signals of known timing and amplitude. Results CalDyn achieved 94.4% sensitivity, 89.9% precision and an F1 score of 0.92. Performance peaked for healthy cardiomyocytes, paced myotubes and action potentials, with lower recall in arrhythmic cardiomyocytes and variable precision in neurons. CalDyn detected candidate low-amplitude diastolic and multicomponent Ca 2+ events in arrhythmic cardiomyocytes, although the biological identity of CalDyn-only events was not independently confirmed. Comparisons with software revealed parameter-specific systematic differences, notably for rise rates and classifications. Action-potential measurements showed limited mean bias but non-negligible limits of agreement. In synthetic signals, amplitude error increased with noise and uncorrected drift, and timing error with low sampling rates. Detection remained stable across moderate parameter variation. Conclusions CalDyn provides an accessible, reproducible and versatile workflow for automated analysis of heterogeneous calcium and electrophysiological signals. With appropriate quality control, it offers a robust alternative to modality-specific tools.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Germline dependence in protein language model retrieval of adaptive immune receptors
item.description: Abstract Protein language models (PLMs) are increasingly used to represent adaptive immune receptors, yet their advantage over classical sequence comparison remains unclear. We benchmarked general and receptor-specific PLMs against classical sequence-comparison methods for antigen-specific nearest-neighbor retrieval across four B- and T-cell receptor databases. Using CDR3 sequences alone, classical methods consistently outperformed general PLMs: BLOSUM62 and Levenshtein exceeded ESM2 variants by 7–12 percentage points in retrieval accuracy. Among receptor-specific models, only SCEPTR and, on one database, TCR2vec matched these baselines, although both additionally encoded V-gene information. AntiBERTa2 and IgBert did not close the performance gap. Using full variable-domain sequences, alignment and PLM performance converged. Germline-reversion, region-masking, and V-gene control analyses indicated that this convergence largely reflected conserved germline-derived context, particularly V-gene identity, with limited evidence for improved extraction of antigen-specific information from the CDRs. Germline dependence also extended to SCEPTR and TCR2vec. Heavily mutated HIV-1 antibodies provided a setting-specific exception to this pattern. Random train-test splits yielded retrieval accuracy 15–28 percentage points higher than clone-aware splits, consistent with optimistic performance estimates due to clonal leakage. These findings emphasize the need for strong sequence-comparison baselines and explicit germline controls when evaluating immune-receptor representations and support clone-aware splitting as a minimum benchmark standard.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Metapath-guided topology and domain knowledge fusion for predicting miRNA–drug–disease triplet resistance and sensitivity associations
item.description: Abstract Accurately predicting drug resistance and sensitivity is critical for understanding disease treatment mechanisms and improving therapeutic strategies. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play essential roles in regulating drug response. However, existing computational methods mainly focus on miRNA–drug pairwise associations and overlook the disease-specific context. In this study, we propose a metapath-guided topology and domain knowledge fusion framework (MTDKF) for predicting miRNA–drug–disease triplet resistance (MRDR) and sensitivity (MRDS) associations. Specifically, we construct a triplet heterogeneous graph to model the interactions among miRNAs, drugs, and diseases. A metapath topology view encoder is designed to capture regulatory patterns between nodes. Additionally, a domain knowledge view encoder is introduced to incorporate sequence, structural, and semantic features of biological entities. These two views are further integrated to learn robust and discriminative representation. We manually curate two benchmark datasets from experimentally validated associations. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that MTDKF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across multiple evaluation metrics. Furthermore, case studies on two breast cancer drugs doxorubicin and tamoxifen demonstrate its potential in discovering novel miRNAs related to drug resistance and sensitivity under disease-specific contexts.

item.title: Nature Biotechnology: Cas12a-based combinatorial knockout screens define the genetic architecture of the DNA damage response
item.description: A genetic interaction map of the DNA damage response (DDR) identifies functional relationships among DDR genes and pathways.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: MultiMHC: a multiscale learning framework integrating sequence and residue contact topology for peptide–MHC binding prediction
item.description: Abstract Accurate prediction of peptide–major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) binding is central to understanding antigen presentation and identifying T-cell epitopes in cancer immunotherapy. Although recent methods have achieved notable progress, most approaches rely predominantly on sequence-based features and only partially capture structural determinants of pMHC recognition. In this study, we present MultiMHC, a multiscale deep learning framework that integrates complementary sequential and biologically-informed residue contact topology for pMHC binding prediction. MultiMHC combines a recurrent neural network to model global sequence context with a graph-based representation to encode residue contact patterns derived from known pMHC binding interfaces. Features from these two pathways are subsequently fused to generate binding predictions across peptides of varying lengths. Benchmark evaluations show that MultiMHC achieves performance comparable to existing state-of-the-art methods, with particularly strong performance in ranking-based assessments. Moreover, evaluation on the Tumor Neoantigen Selection Alliance dataset showed that MultiMHC binding scores can enrich experimentally validated T-cell epitopes among top-ranked candidates, supporting its potential utility as an upstream binding-based filtering step in neoantigen discovery workflows. Together, these results highlight the value of incorporating residue interaction patterns and lightweight structural information into pMHC modeling and establish MultiMHC as a robust and extensive framework for antigen presentation analysis.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Response to comments on “SpatialDG: a novel spatial domain identification method for spatially resolved transcriptomics data based on dual-graph neural network”
item.description: Abstract We respond to concerns regarding reference-label-informed epoch selection in SpatialDG. We acknowledge this limitation and report a matched DLPFC reevaluation of SpatialDG and Spatial-MGCN under the same reference-label-independent checkpoint-selection rule, in which SpatialDG achieved the higher three-seed mean ARI on all 12 slices.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: HEDGEHOG: hierarchical evaluation of drug generators through rigorous filtration
item.description: Abstract Generative molecular models can support early drug discovery by proposing new candidate compounds de novo . In practice, useful candidates must balance target-relevant activity, physicochemical properties, and other multiparameter design constraints. However, standard metrics commonly used to evaluate molecular generators only weakly reflect whether the generated compounds are medicinally plausible and suitable for downstream computation. This can produce an incomplete view of model performance and inefficient use of computational resources. We introduce HEDGEHOG, a configurable six-stage evaluation framework that is constructed as a hit identification workflow: (i) preprocessing; (ii) physicochemical descriptor screening; (iii) structural alerts and graph-sanity checks; (iv) synthesis feasibility; (v) docking; and (vi) 3D pose and interaction checks. We evaluated $22$ generative models in a KRAS G12D case study, using three runs of $1000$ requested generation attempts per model. The models showed different patterns of attrition, and final survival ranged from zero to $127.0 \pm 18.1$ molecules per run. None of the standard metrics showed a significant association with final survival after correction for multiple testing. HEDGEHOG provides a reproducible framework for evaluating molecular generative models under defined screening criteria. The framework identifies stage-wise failure modes across generators and provides a practical basis for developing molecular generators better aligned with early drug discovery.

item.title: Nature Methods: Nondisruptive 3D profiling of combinations of epigenetic marks in single cells
item.description: Epi-PHR is an imaging method that maps combinations of epigenetic marks at single genes while preserving 3D genome structure, revealing how chromatin folding and histone modifications are linked among single-chromatin copies.

item.title: Nature Methods: abcFISH enables multiplexed, single-molecule visualization of circular RNA spatial heterogeneity
item.description: abcFISH is an imaging method for multiplexed, single‑molecule circular RNA detection in cells and in vivo, revealing single-cell expression heterogeneity and direct therapeutic efficacy of circular aptamers.

item.title: Nature Methods: Automated identification of individual birds by song enables multi-year recapture from passive acoustic monitoring data
item.description: A machine learning-based method distinguishes individual ovenbirds in the wild by their distinct vocalizations, collected by passive acoustic recording.

item.title: Nature Methods: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC
item.description: DIRAC is a geometric deep learning model that enables both vertical and horizontal integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: spOT-NMF: gene expression deconvolution via optimal transport with proximity-aware niche mapping for spatial transcriptomics
item.description: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics enables direct profiling of cellular organization within intact tissues, yet two challenges limit its full exploitation: accurate reference-free deconvolution of mixed expression signals (including species-admixed models such as xenografts), and lack of tools that can translate per-spot program usage values into spatial niches. We developed spOT-NMF, an optimal transport-based non-negative matrix factorization method that replaces standard reconstruction loss with the Wasserstein distance to disentangle mixed signals without requiring matched single-cell atlases. While the generalized OT-NMF factorization is applicable to any expression matrix, a proximity-based niche inference module further translates program co-usage from spatial transcriptomes into directional co-occurrence networks that define tissue compartments and their boundaries. Benchmarking across five gold-standard datasets spanning sub-cellular to multi-cellular resolutions, multiple platforms, and two-species admixture scenarios, spOT-NMF ranks first among reference-free methods, with particular advantage under the signal imbalance conditions characteristic of xenografts. We show that reference-free deconvolution recovers cell populations absent from matched single-cell atlases, highlighting the value of unsupervised analysis. Applied to glioblastoma xenografts and human colorectal cancer, spOT-NMF reveals spatially restricted interferon signaling, invasion routes, and CAF–tumor boundaries. spOT-NMF is available as an open-source Python package with GPU, CPU, and HPC support.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Machine learning for RNA–small molecule interactions: methodologies, evaluation, and future directions
item.description: Abstract RNA is emerging as a compelling therapeutic target due to its rich structural diversity and central involvement in gene regulation, splicing, translation, and cellular signaling. Alongside advances in structural biology, computational approaches, especially machine learning and deep learning, have transformed the systematic analysis of RNA–small molecule interactions. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey of computational methods for RNA–small molecule interaction prediction, with a particular emphasis on three core tasks: binding site prediction, binding preference prediction, and binding pose prediction. We first summarize the data resources commonly used to support these tasks and outline molecular representations that capture RNA structural features and the chemical properties of small molecules. We then review a spectrum of computational approaches for the above three tasks, ranging from statistical methods and traditional machine learning to deep learning. We further evaluate representative methods for each task, providing insights into their respective strengths and limitations. Finally, we highlight open challenges in current research on RNA–small molecule interactions, including limited data availability, the black-box nature of the models, and the growing need for generative modeling. We discuss emerging directions such as data augmentation, model interpretability, and RNA-targeted small-molecule design as promising pathways to address these challenges and advance rational RNA-targeted drug discovery.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Inferring causal networks for genomic trios with high-dimensional confounding variables
item.description: Abstract Causal structure inference under the principle of Mendelian randomization (PMR) enables the study of causal relationships between two molecular phenotypes (e.g. gene expression) by leveraging genetic variants as instrumental variables to impose constraints on edge direction. In practice, inference is often affected by numerous confounding variables, such as other genes, other processes and demographic variables, making it essential to robustly account for confounders. However, existing methods have limited ability to accommodate high-dimensional confounding. Here, we introduce Mendelian randomization for genomic networks (MRGN), a regression-based method under the PMR for inferring causal models in genomic trios from individual-level data while accounting for many confounders. MRGN extends beyond the canonical mediation model to distinguish among multiple causal relationships. By prioritizing conditional independence tests given the genetic variant and confounders, MRGN can detect causal relationships between phenotypes even when their marginal association is weak. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate improved inference accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency over existing approaches. We further apply MRGN to data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression Consortium to investigate how genetic variants may regulate gene expression in cis and trans.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Identifying multi-omics spatial domains via masked autoencoder and diffusion-based latent regularization with SpaMEDM
item.description: Abstract Spatial multi-omics data provide complementary molecular views of tissue organization. However, their integration remains challenging due to data sparsity, technical noise, and modality-specific distributions. Here, we present Spatial Masked autoEncoder and Diffusion-based Model (SpaMEDM), an end-to-end graph representation learning framework that augments a dual-attention graph-integration backbone with masked reconstruction and diffusion-based latent noise-prediction regularization. In the masked track, randomly masked spot features are recovered by leveraging modality- and graph-specific neighborhood information. In parallel, Gaussian perturbations are applied to modality-specific latent representations at randomly sampled noise levels, and a spatial-graph-informed network is trained to predict the injected noise. This diffusion-based objective is used exclusively during training to encourage robustness to latent perturbations, rather than to perform iterative reverse diffusion or sampling during inference. Furthermore, cosine-based paired-spot directional alignment and adjacency reconstruction encourage compatible cross-modality representations and preservation of the selected graph structure. SpaMEDM flexibly supports purely spatial, dual feature–spatial, and modality-specific feature-pruned spatial graph configurations. Evaluations across diverse spatial multi-omics datasets demonstrate competitive spatial-domain identification performance and produce integrated embeddings that facilitate downstream exploratory analyses.

item.title: Bioinformatics: scPhyloGRN: gene regulatory network inference guided by lineage topology in single-cell developmental data
item.description: Abstract Motivation Gene regulatory network (GRN) inference from single-cell transcriptomes is complicated by expression patterns associated with both cell state and shared ancestry. Cellular phylogenies provide developmental context, but incorporating relationships among individual cells into gene-level regulatory inference remains challenging. Results We present scPhyloGRN, a supervised framework that integrates single-cell gene expression with cellular phylogeny to prioritize directed transcription factor (TF)–target candidates within the observed gene set. The framework maps cell ancestry to gene associations that guide graph construction, attention in a dual-stream encoder, and lineage-consistency regularization. We evaluated scPhyloGRN against 10 methods across 17 dataset–reference settings spanning four mouse embryos and one Caenorhabditis elegans dataset. scPhyloGRN showed an overall advantage in regulatory edge prioritization, supported by additional evaluations using shared candidate spaces. Removing lineage information reduced AUPRC in the ablation analyses, while branch-level and regulator-level analyses showed improved ranking and recovery of reference-supported regulatory candidates. Availability and implementation Source code and analysis workflows are available at https://github.com/Maria0852/scPhyloGRN , with a versioned archive at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22793831 .

item.title: Nature Methods: RobPicker: a meta-learning framework for robust identification of macromolecules in cryo-electron tomograms
item.description: RobPicker improves cryo-ET particle picking by correcting noisy labels and reweighting rare species, enabling robust detection of small macromolecules across diverse datasets.

item.title: Nature Methods: Head-mounted camera for reconstructing outdoor behavior in freely flying birds
item.description: A head-mounted camera in combination with drone-based mapping of the environment allows reconstruction of the flight trajectory and behavior such as prey capture in freely flying birds such as the Harris’s hawk.

item.title: Nature Methods: Limitations of de novo peptide sequencing in resolving sequence ambiguity
item.description: A benchmark of eight deep learning tools that sequence peptides directly from mass spectra (de novo) shows that their errors mostly stem from incomplete spectra, not model design, calling for tools that flag uncertain regions instead of guessing full sequences.

item.title: Nature Methods: Selective profiling of translationally active tRNAs and their dynamics under stress
item.description: tRIBO-seq distinguishes between ribosome-associated tRNAs and total tRNAs using nanopore sequencing, thus revealing their potentially distinct abundance, modification and fragmentation patterns in various conditions.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: MAGE: an efficient algorithm for identifying Maximal Age-indexed GEne sets
item.description: Abstract Aging alters transcriptional regulation in a tissue- and time-specific manner, reshaping gene regulatory networks and shifting regulatory influence dynamics. Traditional in silico influence maximization methods often rely on static gene expression snapshots and fail to capture gene-to-gene influence variations over time. To address this, we introduce the Age Index , a network-based metric that quantifies time-varying gene influence. We define the Maximal and Minimal Age Index Problems (MAP$^{+}$ and MAP$^{-}$) as the tasks of identifying gene sets with the highest and lowest Age Index, and prove these problems are NP-hard. To solve them, we develop MAGE (Maximal Age-Index Algorithm), a stochastic method that iteratively constructs gene sets by prioritizing genes likely to optimize the Age Index. MAGE identifies statistically significant gene sets at the genome scale, with strong literature support, highlighting its potential to uncover age-sensitive regulatory mechanisms.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: HiCP2GAN: a plug and play foundation model-based GAN for Hi-C enhancement
item.description: Abstract The 3D organization of chromatin shapes gene regulation and cellular function, and Hi-C has become the primary technique for mapping chromatin interactions genome-wide. However, high-resolution data remain costly and scarce, leaving many studies with sparse contact maps that limit downstream analysis. Deep learning methods, especially generative adversarial networks (GANs), have shown promise for enhancing low-resolution Hi-C data, but most existing GAN-based approaches rely on custom discriminators trained from scratch, which can yield unstable training and limited generalization. Hi-C foundation models pretrained on large-scale data capture rich, transferable representations of chromatin structure, yet their use as discriminators within adversarial enhancement frameworks had not been explored. We introduce HiCP2GAN, a plug-and-play GAN that employs a pretrained Vision Transformer-based Hi-C foundation model as its discriminator. The discriminator was pretrained on 118 million Hi-C patches across diverse species and cell types, providing biologically meaningful gradients for adversarial supervision. The framework is generator-agnostic: any compatible Hi-C resolution enhancement architecture can serve as the generator, enabling fair comparison across methods. The encoder phase of the foundation model was adapted as a discriminator backbone, finetuning the first few layers from the input while freezing the deeper transformer layers to preserve pretrained knowledge while allowing task-specific adaptation. Experiments across various cell lines show that HiCP2GAN outperforms traditional GAN-based methods in most settings and improves the reconstruction quality and biological reproducibility of existing Hi-C enhancement models in most evaluated cases. HiCP2GAN is publicly available at https://github.com/OluwadareLab/HiCP2GAN .

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: IsoPrism predicts isoform usage from short-read transcriptomes through structure-guided competitive allocation
item.description: Abstract Short-read (SR) single-cell and spatial transcriptomics characterize gene expression but provide limited resolution of within-gene isoform usage. Here we present IsoPrism, a structure-guided competitive allocation framework that predicts isoform proportions from gene-level expression. IsoPrism combines individual expression and local expression context with transcript structural annotations, using shared iterative updates to preserve non-negative, gene-normalized proportions. Joint supervision from individual long-read (LR) counts and group-level isoform usage enables prediction in samples without matched LR measurements. Across five transfer scenarios derived from three paired transcriptomic resources, IsoPrism achieved the highest mean dominant isoform accuracy, compositional similarity, and cluster-level allocation correlation among eight evaluated methods. Ablation analyses supported complementary contributions from structural queries, expression context, iterative allocation, and dual-resolution supervision. Applied to a developing mouse cortex atlas, IsoPrism identified stage- and cell-type-associated isoform-usage patterns, including variation in the predicted relative usage of two Pkm transcripts. IsoPrism enables isoform-usage analysis of SR transcriptomes by transferring information from paired LR references, extending the analytical value of existing single-cell and spatial gene-expression atlases.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: ADInteractome: discovering Alzheimer’s disease-associated gene interactions from single-nucleus RNA-seq data through neural interaction states
item.description: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid $\beta $ plaques and tau tangles, yet its molecular mechanisms remain elusive. Advances in single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) have provided profound insights into the cellular heterogeneity of AD-associated brains. In this study, we introduce ADInteractome, an interpretable artificial intelligence framework designed to discover gene interactions associated with AD directly from the internal state of neural networks trained on the snRNA-seq data of brain cells. The method is based on the intuition that if a neural network can accurately classify cells from AD and non-AD donors based on their snRNA-seq data, then its internal interaction states, reflecting interaction patterns within the gene expression data, are informative for identifying biologically meaningful gene interactions. Applied to a large-scale snRNA-seq dataset from the Seattle Alzheimer’s Disease Brain Cell Atlas, ADInteractome reveals cell-type-specific and AD-associated gene circuits supported by existing literature. The results were further supported by our virtual knock-out and knock-in experiments, a novel concept to probe our findings through a data-driven approach. Compared with traditional co-expression network methods, it achieves stronger enrichment for known AD-associated gene interactions and uncovers novel interaction patterns. These findings highlight the potential of interpretable AI approaches for elucidating complex molecular interactions in neurodegenerative disease.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Multi-omics survival prediction under modality incompleteness via dynamic modality graphs and product-of-experts fusion
item.description: Abstract Multi-omics data integration provides rich complementary information for cancer survival prediction, yet modality incompleteness is pervasive in real-world medical data and undermines the stability and applicability of existing models. To address this challenge, we propose DMG-PoE, a robust learning framework for multi-omics survival prediction. The framework introduces a dynamic modality graph (DMG) that propagates complementary information across modality nodes to compensate for missing inputs, combined with an uncertainty-aware product-of-experts (PoE) fusion mechanism that adaptively weights each modality by its estimated precision, and a consistency-constrained training strategy that stabilizes predictions across varying modality subsets. Systematic evaluation on the SurvBoard benchmark across 10 TCGA cancer types and seven omics modalities demonstrates that DMG-PoE achieves the highest average C-index under both the standard setting (complete-modality training/testing) and the missing-augmented setting (training additionally includes real incomplete samples and nonclinical modality dropout, with complete-only testing); controlled per-modality masking experiments validate effective test-time recovery in 22/24 cancer-modality combinations, and cross-cohort transfer with only two of seven modalities available further confirms generalization under severe input restriction.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: AxialTAD: an axial contrast architecture for TAD boundary prediction from Hi-C
item.description: Abstract Topologically associating domains (TADs) are fundamental units of 3D chromatin organization, and accurate identification of TAD boundaries from Hi-C contact matrices remains an active challenge. Recent deep learning approaches have advanced substantially, but these rely on increasingly large architectures, raising the question of how much of this capacity boundary-centric analysis requires. Here we propose AxialTAD, a compact deep learning model centered on an Axial Contrast Module (ACM) that explicitly encodes directional contrast in contact intensity along the row and column axes of local Hi-C patches, an operator aligned with the geometric signature of TAD boundaries. Evaluated on four human cell lines (GM12878, HeLa-S3, IMR-90, K562) within cell lines and under leave-one-cell-out generalization, AxialTAD performed comparably with a recent convolutional neural network (CNN)+Transformer baseline (deepTAD) while using 76%–80% fewer trainable parameters (113K–137K versus 571K). A parameter-matched conventional CNN achieved similar F1 to AxialTAD in the human 25 kb experiments. When trained and evaluated within each of two mouse datasets, AxialTAD outperformed both this control and deepTAD. Orthogonal validation against CTCF and cohesin ChIP-seq supported the biological plausibility of the predicted boundaries. These results indicate that, within the range of architectures examined, a large architecture is not necessary to reach this level of boundary prediction.

item.title: Bioinformatics: TRACER: twin-contrastive learning for fine-grained and rare spatial domain identification in spatial transcriptomics
item.description: Abstract Motivation Fine-grained and rare spatial domains are difficult to identify in spatial transcriptomics because they contain few spots, show subtle transcriptional differences, and are strongly influenced by neighboring regions. Results We present TRACER, a twin-contrastive learning framework that integrates a graph convolutional autoencoder with neighborhood-aware instance-level and cluster-level contrastive learning. By jointly preserving local spatial continuity and enhancing domain separability, TRACER achieved competitive and generally robust performance compared with representative spatial domain identification methods across multiple spatially resolved transcriptomic datasets, including human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex generated by 10× Visium, mouse brain datasets generated by STARmap, osmFISH, and BARISTAseq, and human breast cancer. TRACER recovered major cortical and anatomical structures, improved the identification of rare or transitional domains in the mouse somatosensory cortex, and revealed candidate functionally distinct small domains within a broadly annotated breast cancer region. Availability and implementation The source code of TRACER is available at https://github.com/luxin-heart/TRACER .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Domain-aware enzyme classification via multiple instance learning
item.description: Abstract Motivation Accurate Enzyme Commission (EC) number prediction is fundamental to protein function annotation and metabolic pathway reconstruction. Recent methods based on protein language model embeddings or 3D structure have improved EC prediction, but important limitations remain. Whole-sequence embeddings can dilute local functional signals, such as catalytic residues and functional domains, whereas structure-based methods depend on accurate protein structures and are therefore difficult to apply broadly. Results We present MIL-BC, a multiple instance learning framework for EC prediction that models each protein as a bag of domains rather than a single sequence-level object. This design is motivated by the observation that enzymatic function is often determined by constituent functional domains instead of the full-length sequence alone. Domain instances are generated automatically using our DCTdomain algorithm, avoiding dependence on curated domain annotations. MIL-BC aggregates domain-level evidence into protein-level EC predictions and assigns interpretable weights to domains that contribute most strongly to each prediction. We further combine the domain embedding with global embedding in MIL-BC+. MIL-BC+ achieved F1 improvements of 0.03–0.17 over the sequence-based baseline on all four test sets. The largest gains were observed for proteins with multiple enzymatic functions, where domain-level modeling better separates mixed functional signals. These results show that domain-centric multiple instance learning is an accurate and interpretable strategy for enzyme classification. By improving EC prediction without requiring structural data or curated domain labels, MIL-BC provides a scalable framework for large-scale protein function annotation. Availability and implementation Code is available as a GitHub repository at https://github.com/omics-ai/enzyme-mil.git .

item.title: Bioinformatics: SiSaNA: a Python-based command line interface for single-sample network analysis
item.description: Abstract Motivation Reconstructing and analyzing single-sample regulatory networks has proven useful for understanding mechanisms of regulatory biology and its disruption in disease but traditionally required a fair amount of programming experience and work from the user. Results Here, we present Single-Sample Network Analysis (SiSaNA), a workflow that removes the need of prior programming experience and allows for single-sample regulatory network reconstruction and analysis, all via a command line interface. Using example input files, we walk the user through a tutorial on how to run the SiSaNA pipeline, interpret the results, and obtain high-quality figures summarized in a single HTML file as output. Availability and implementation SiSaNA is freely available to install with pip via the Python Package Index. It is additionally available on GitHub at https://github.com/kuijjerlab/sisana . Example input files can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17190642 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: PRIDA: cross-domain protein–RNA interaction prediction based on biological language models and conditional domain-adversarial learning
item.description: Abstract Motivation The interaction between RNA and proteins is a complex process that involves atom-level details and dynamic changes. Accurate prediction of protein–RNA interactions helps researchers to develop protein-targeted small nucleic acid drugs. However, the scarcity of protein–RNA complexes and experimental data limits the ability of existing data-driven supervised learning methods to learn latent patterns, leading to limited performance. Results In this study, we propose PRIDA (Protein–RNA Interaction prediction based on Domain-Adversarial learning), a protein–RNA interaction framework that combines bilinear attention with conditional domain-adversarial learning. Powered by pretrained protein and RNA language models, PRIDA improves interaction prediction under protein-level distribution shifts and limited labeled data. By integrating PRIDA with Monte Carlo Tree Search, we apply it to a virtual screening pipeline to generate RNA aptamer candidates for specific target proteins. Experimental results show that PRIDA achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction and provides effective guidance for RNA aptamer virtual screening. Availability and implementation The data and source code of the proposed method are available at GitHub ( https://github.com/zhouyyang/PRIDA ) and Zenodo ( https://zenodo.org/records/23644677 ).

item.title: Bioinformatics: Verix: a toolkit for benchmarking and harmonization of complex structural variants
item.description: Abstract Summary Complex structural variants (CSVs) represent a critical yet under-characterized class of large-scale genomic rearrangements. CSV discovery requires not only the accurate detection of individual breakpoints but also their assembly into a single, structurally resolved CSV event. However, CSV method development is currently limited by a diagnostic gap: existing SV evaluation frameworks are designed for single-interval or single-junction SVs and cannot quantify multi-breakpoint CSV reconstruction fidelity or systematically distinguish between different types of reconstruction errors, such as over-segmentation or collapse of independent breakpoints. Here we present Verix, a comprehensive toolkit designed for the fine-grained evaluation and integration of CSVs. Verix introduces granular diagnostic metrics that enable researchers to thoroughly characterize CSV predictions and stratify performance based on breakpoint sensitivity, precision, and structural integrity. In addition to pairwise callset-to-truthset comparisons, Verix also provides an intra- and inter-callset harmonization module for generating consensus calls for a single tool’s output or across disparate discovery pipelines. As such, Verix provides the infrastructure needed to rigorously evaluate and reconcile CSV calls, accelerating the standardization of CSV discovery in both research and clinical settings. Availability and implementation Verix is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/PopicLab/verix and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22998063 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Starlng: STability Analysis of coRegulated ‘Nests’ of Genes
item.description: Abstract Motivation Single-cell assays (both single and multi-omics) represent the state-of-the-art for detailed characterization of cell phenotypes, a task frequently initialized with the identification of groups of genes linked to well-defined, stable subpopulations of cells. Gene expression covariation patterns are simplified precursors of Gene Regulatory Networks (GRNs) and play a crucial role in inferring causality and dynamics within GRNs. However, current gene clustering methods struggle to capture spatial organization and relationship dynamics along developmental trajectories, while remaining vulnerable to noise and algorithmic stochasticity. Results Expanding on the ClustAssess framework, which shifted the cluster-centric assessment of populations of cells to an element-centric perspective, we propose to assess the covariation induced by gene graph clustering. The Starlng (abbrev) framework provides an optimized, interactive environment for the identification of the filtered modules. The pipeline identifies the stable configuration of clustering parameters and robust gene modules (nests of genes), followed by the removal of the outlier clusters based on the pseudotime variance. We illustrate Starlng on the identification of reliable, reproducible communities of genes, as well as reveal unbiased hierarchical relationships between higher level cell clusters and more granular subgroups of genes. Availability and implementation Starlng is implemented in R and freely available at https://github.com/Core-Bioinformatics/Starlng .

item.title: Bioinformatics: rustybam: a composable toolkit for alignment analysis and visualization with SafFire
item.description: Abstract Summary We present rustybam , a Rust-based command-line toolkit for CIGAR-aware manipulation of PAF and BAM alignments, and SafFire , a browser-based tool for interactive genome comparison visualization with annotation overlays. rustybam’s composable subcommands provide overlap resolution, coordinate liftover, alignment splitting at structural variants, scaffolding, and identity statistics. Availability and implementation Both tools are open source under the MIT license. rustybam is available via Bioconda ( https://anaconda.org/bioconda/rustybam ), crates.io, and GitHub ( https://github.com/vollgerlab/rustybam ). SafFire is hosted at https://vollgerlab.com/SafFire/ with source code at https://github.com/vollgerlab/SafFire . Archived versions are available on Zenodo: rustybam ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4654875 ) and SafFire ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5765964 ).

item.title: Bioinformatics: CSK-DDI: compensating structural incompleteness with knowledge graph world knowledge for drug–drug interaction modeling
item.description: Abstract Motivation Drug–drug interaction (DDI) prediction is critical for drug safety, yet existing methods suffer from structural incompleteness in drug representation. Motif and molecular graph encodings capture local substructures and global topology but remain confined to the closed structural space of individual molecules, lacking cross-entity and contextual information and leading to limited generalization, especially in cold-start scenarios. To address this issue, we propose CSK-DDI (Compensating Structural Incompleteness with Knowledge Graph World Knowledge for Drug–Drug Interaction Modeling), a multimodal framework that jointly encodes motif-level chemical patterns, molecular graph topology, and biomedical knowledge graph (KG) context as complementary drug representations. The KG encodes drugs’ contextual positions and relational semantics through multi-entity and multi-relation connections, providing global cross-entity and cross-semantic information that complements structural representations. The resulting fusion captures local chemical patterns, global topology, and biomedical context in a unified embedding. Results CSK-DDI employs a cross-attention mechanism to enable multi-view interaction among motif, molecular graph, and KG representations, producing unified structure-aware and context-aware drug embeddings. To improve robustness under sparse conditions, the model further incorporates a cold-start-oriented representation enhancement strategy. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with particularly notable gains in cold-start scenarios. Availability and implementation Source code and data are available at https://github.com/cgwcbz2/CSK-DDI and on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21415769 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Ernie-Switcher: RNA foundation model-guided design of programmable RNA devices in a navigable landscape
item.description: Abstract Motivation Recent advances in biological foundation models have enabled new opportunities for data-driven molecular engineering. However, designing programmable RNA devices remains challenging because of the vast, nonlinear sequence-structure-function landscape. Here, we present Ernie-Switcher, a deep learning framework built upon the RNA foundation model (RNAErnie), comprising three coupled components: (i) integration of RNAErnie-derived sequence-phenotype representations for realistic design generation and filtering, (ii) characterization of RNA landscape navigability as a theoretical basis for sequence optimization, and (iii) incorporation of biophysical constraints to maintain optimization trajectories within biologically plausible bounds. Results We validated Ernie-Switcher using RNA toehold switches. Theoretically, the observed lower bound on threshold navigability (86.4%) of the RNA landscape supports the theoretical feasibility of RNA switch sequence optimization. Experimentally, the optimized toehold switches achieved ON/OFF expression ratios of up to 35-fold in Escherichia coli . Collectively, RNAErnie-guided sequence optimization provides a scalable strategy for engineering high-performance RNA devices. To facilitate broad adoption, we deployed Ernie-Switcher as a freely accessible web platform. Availability and implementation The Python code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/zhutiblah/Ernie-Switcher and are archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21859277 . The RNA toehold switch design platform is available at https://ernie-switcher.bioinformatics-syn.org/ .

item.title: Bioinformatics: GBZ-base and GAF-base: indexed pangenome file formats
item.description: Abstract Motivation Existing pangenome file formats are designed for batch processing. Graphs must be loaded into memory, and alignment files must be read sequentially. Indexed file formats that can be used directly from disk would be more appropriate for interactive applications. Results We propose GBZ-base and GAF-base—SQLite-backed file formats comparable to GBZ and GAF. GBZ-base supports efficient extraction of local subgraphs, and GAF-base lets us extract all alignments to the subgraph. Additionally, GAF-base is smaller than any other file format for sequence-to-graph alignments. Availability and implementation From https://github.com/jltsiren/gbz-base and https://crates.io/crates/gbz-base under the MIT license.

item.title: Bioinformatics: Multi-view state-space modeling for zero-shot circRNA–miRNA interaction prediction
item.description: Abstract Motivation CircRNA–miRNA interactions (CMIs) play regulatory roles in human diseases and provide clues for therapeutic target discovery. However, most existing prediction methods rely on circRNA–miRNA pairs and overlook disease-level regulatory contexts, which limits their ability to characterize cross-pathway dependencies in zero-shot inference. Results We propose MV-S 2 M, a multi-view state-space modeling framework that integrates molecular attributes to enhance relational reasoning, enabling zero-shot CMI prediction. Specifically, MV-S 2 M performs structure-aware diffusion to enrich molecular priors and constructs disease-mediated semantic subgraphs. It then incorporates state-space modeling to capture long-range dependencies and view-specific regulatory patterns. The learned multi-view representations are fused through a linear projection and fed into an MLP for CMI prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that MV-S 2 M achieves state-of-the-art performance under both zero-shot and conventional settings. Cold-start evaluations reveal distinct generalization behavior across different unseen-entity settings. Case studies illustrate the contribution of meta-path-guided semantic subgraphs to CMI prediction. Availability and implementation The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/591286260/MV and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22858403 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Large-scale semantic indexing of Spanish biomedical literature using contrastive transfer learning
item.description: Abstract Motivation The exponential growth of biomedical literature has made automatic indexing essential for advancing biomedical research. While automatic indexing has made strides in English biomedical literature, there has been limited research on non-English biomedical texts due to insufficient high-quality training data. Results We propose BERTDeCS, a novel deep learning framework for automatically indexing Spanish biomedical literature using contrastive transfer learning. BERTDeCS utilizes a multilingual BERT (M-BERT) to generate multi-language representations and adapts M-BERT for Spanish biomedical literature domain through contrastive learning. Additionally, BERTDeCS enhances its semantic indexing capabilities on Spanish biomedical literature by leveraging enriched English annotated literature in MEDLINE through transfer learning. Experimental results on Spanish datasets demonstrate that BERTDeCS outperforms state-of-the-art indexing methods, achieving top performance in the MESINESP and MESINESP2 Tasks on medical semantic indexing in Spanish within the BioASQ challenge. Additional experiments on Portuguese provide preliminary evidence that BERTDeCS can transfer to a closely related language sharing substantial lexical and biomedical terminology with Spanish. Availability The source code is available at https://github.com/yourh/BERTDeCS and at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23212468 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: SomatiX: accurate and efficient somatic SNV detection from matched tumor-normal long-read DNA sequencing
item.description: Abstract Motivation Accurate somatic single-nucleotide variant (SNV) calling from matched tumor-normal long-read DNA sequencing remains challenging because sequencing errors, variable tumor purity, tumor-in-normal contamination, and low variant allele fractions (VAFs) can obscure tumor-specific signals. Although recent deep-learning methods have improved long-read somatic variant calling, robust low-VAF detection and efficient genome-scale analysis remain important methodological challenges. Results We present SomatiX, a deep-learning method for somatic SNV detection from matched tumor-normal long-read DNA sequencing data, built on an allele-aware pileup representation. In comprehensive cancer benchmark analyses across diverse cell-line datasets, sequencing contexts, VAF bins, and minimum variant-supporting read thresholds, SomatiX outperformed DeepSomatic and ClairS in F1 score across most Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) benchmark conditions and achieved competitive performance on Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) data. Across the held-out chromosome 1 cancer cell-line benchmarks, at the threshold of ≥3 variant-supporting reads and a VAF ≥0.05, SomatiX achieved mean F1 scores of 0.986 for ONT data and 0.988 for PacBio data. SomatiX showed particularly strong performance for low-VAF SNVs in ONT data while using a compact model and achieving the fastest runtime among the evaluated tools. Availability and implementation SomatiX is available at https://github.com/colinliuzelin/SomatiX and archived at Zenodo under DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22062438 . The repository includes source code, trained models, and benchmarking scripts.

item.title: Bioinformatics: AbLWR: a context-aware listwise ranking framework for antibody-antigen binding affinity prediction via positive-unlabeled learning
item.description: Abstract Motivation Accurate prediction of antibody-antigen binding affinity is fundamental to therapeutic design and the rapid response to evolving pathogens. However, current computational approaches predominantly formulate this as a point-wise regression task. This paradigm struggles to discriminate subtle affinity differences among highly homologous variants and lacks the global context necessary to effectively prioritize top-tier candidates. Furthermore, the field is severely constrained by label sparsity. Although sequence data is abundant, experimentally verified affinities are scarce, leaving a massive pool of unverified antibody-antigen structural interactions unexploited by standard supervised paradigms. Results We propose AbLWR (Antibody-antigen binding affinity Listwise Ranking), a novel framework that reformulates the conventional affinity regression task as a listwise ranking problem to directly optimize candidate prioritization. To mitigate label sparsity, AbLWR incorporates a Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning mechanism, leveraging a dual-level contrastive objective and meta-optimized label refinement to distill robust structural representations from vast unlabeled data. To accommodate antigenic variation, we employ a homologous antigen sampling strategy coupled with a Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) module, which explicitly models inter-sample dependencies within training lists to capture subtle affinity nuances. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that AbLWR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art sequence-, structure-, and complex-based baselines. It improves the Full Rank Accuracy (FRA) by approximately 8% compared to the strongest baseline in randomized cross-validation, and exhibits strong robustness in out-of-distribution scenarios involving distinct antigen and antibody clusters. Case studies on Influenza Viruses and Human Interleukin-33 further validate its practical utility. Specifically, AbLWR successfully tracks affinity drops caused by antigenic drift and immediately captures optimal binders in simulated wet-lab screening. Availability Source code and datasets are freely available at https://github.com/Josie-xufan/AbLWR .

item.title: Bioinformatics: BioHarness: substrate-aware evidence assembly for biomedical question answering across literature, knowledge bases, and biological atlases
item.description: Abstract Motivation Biomedical question answering often requires evidence beyond topically retrieved literature, including gene alias resolution, database identifier normalization, and atlas-derived biological measurements. However, existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems typically follow a fixed workflow and lack an explicit mechanism for deciding when retrieved text is sufficient, when biomedical entity mapping is needed, or when executable evidence assembly over structured measurements should be invoked. This motivates a substrate-aware large language model (LLM) harness that selectively assembles sufficient evidence by combining literature retrieval, biomedical entity mapping, and access to atlas-derived measurements. Results We introduce BioHarness, an LLM harness for staged biomedical evidence assembly across literature retrieval, biomedical entity-mapping resources, and atlas-derived structured measurements. Across 22 123 biomedical QA items spanning seven answer formats, BioHarness improves the pooled score from 62.2 to 67.2 over the strongest baseline. Ablations, case studies, and backbone-scaling analyses show that these gains arise from repairing evidence-substrate mismatches through reranking, entity grounding, and structured measurement access, rather than from indiscriminately invoking more reasoning steps, retrieving additional literature, or relying on a particular answer-model scale. Comparisons with the frontier models and harness show that BioHarness, despite using an open-weight backbone with only 3B active parameters, approaches frontier-level performance on selected literature QA tasks and outperforms frontier harnesses without web access on biomedical identifier and locus lookup. Availability and implementation The source code, reproducible benchmarking scripts, and processed benchmark data required to reproduce all results in this study are publicly available under an open-source license, together with the exat configuration, model versions, and decoding settings used in our experiments. In addition, we developed a prototype web demo ( https://xcompass.scimatrix.cn/ ) that illustrates how BioHarness can be used in an interactive biomedical QA setting.

item.title: Bioinformatics: LRP2: a proteogenomics pipeline for long-read informed protein isoform analysis and discovery
item.description: Abstract Summary Most human genes produce multiple RNA isoforms, yet it remains unclear which isoforms are translated into stable, functional proteins. Long-read RNA sequencing resolves full-length transcript structures and, when paired with mass spectrometry, can provide empirical evidence of isoform translation. Despite this opportunity, comprehensive workflows integrating isoform discovery, open reading frame prediction, peptide identification, and protein inference remain limited, leaving users to handle these steps piecemeal. Here, we present LRP2, a modular, end-to-end long-read proteogenomics pipeline built in Nextflow. LRP2 scales transcript discovery to hundreds of samples via PacBio’s latest Isocall tool, removes technical artifacts with SQANTI QC, generates and classifies predicted proteomes via CPAT and SQANTI Protein, performs multi-group differential expression and usage analysis via edgeR, DRIMSeq, and a long-read adaptation of LeafCutter, and integrates protein-level evidence from DDA and DIA MS data through FragPipe. For cross-dataset comparison of novel isoforms, LRP2 employs deterministic splice junction, coordinate-based isoform identifiers. Used as an integrated pipeline, LRP2 enables the detection of novel peptides and improves protein isoform inference to confirm protein isoform translation. Availability and implementation LRP2 is freely available as a modular Nextflow pipeline at https://github.com/sheynkman-lab/LRP2 (v2.0.0, archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22795865 ). LRP2 supports Docker, Apptainer/Singularity, and Conda environments with GENCODE references.

item.title: Bioinformatics: From SELEX to sequencing: uncovering enriched aptamers with next-generation sequencing and bioinformatics
item.description: Abstract Motivation The combinatorial chemistry process called systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) enables the selection of aptamers against different targets. The integration of next-generation sequencing (NGS) into SELEX workflows represents a powerful strategy to enhance the identification and prioritization of target-binding aptamers. In this study, we present an optimized computational approach for the NGS-based analysis of enriched aptamer pools generated through SELEX. It encompasses sequencing library preparation, sequence data preprocessing, clustering, multiple sequence alignment, phylogenetic analysis, and secondary structure prediction. Results To identify target-specific aptamers, two comparative analysis strategies were implemented. In the first strategy, sequences detected in the negative selection pool were removed from the positive selection pool to eliminate nonspecific binders, resulting in six distinct sequence clusters. In the second approach, all sequences were retained, and cluster distributions were compared between the positive and negative selection pools, identifying seven clusters in the positive and six in the negative pool. Phylogenetic relationships and structural predictions enabled the selection of promising candidates, which were prioritized based on secondary structure, sequence abundance, and genetic distance from nonspecific binders. Binding specificity was assessed through dot blot assays, confirming that the selected aptamers exhibited strong specific binding to the target protein. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the NGS-guided workflow for aptamer discovery and highlight its value in streamlining candidate selection for downstream functional validation. Availability and Implementation The data underlying this article will be shared on reasonable request to the corresponding author.

item.title: Bioinformatics: XenoMix: estimating mouse content from DNA methylation data of Patient-Derived Xenograft models
item.description: Abstract Summary DNA methylation microarrays enable cost-effective, high-throughput profiling of human and mouse samples and are widely used to study epigenetic alterations in cancer. Patient-Derived Xenograft (PDX) models complement this approach by preserving primary tumor characteristics while enabling in vivo studies of drug response and therapy resistance. However, it remains difficult to quantify mouse DNA contamination in PDX DNA methylation data generated using microarrays. We present XenoMix, a light-weight computational tool for quantifying mouse DNA contamination directly from DNA methylation data in PDX models. XenoMix leverages the high sequence homology between human and mouse genomes to detect and quantify unexpected signal contributions originating from mouse DNA. Using ground truth mixtures, XenoMix achieved Pearson’s correlation coefficients higher than 0.99. When applied to PDX data, we identified varying levels of mouse contamination originating from biological and technological variability. XenoMix establishes a critical quality control step in DNA methylation analysis of PDX models, and we show that the estimated contamination can be incorporated as a confounding variable in downstream analyses. Availability and implementation XenoMix is available as a standalone R package from https://git.dkfz.de/b370/scepigen/XenoMix and as a module in the RnBeads software package.
