item.title: Bioinformatics: Integrating complementary datasets for constructing microbiome–metabolome–disease pathways
item.description: Abstract Motivation Microbiome–metabolome–disease pathways play a central role in host health, but studying them is limited by the data available. Large clinical microbiome cohorts often lack metabolomic measurements, while multi-omics studies with paired profiles are typically small or incompletely phenotyped. Combining such complementary datasets is challenging: the metabolite is not measured in the clinical cohort, microbiome data are high-dimensional and compositional, and log-ratio analyses depend on an arbitrarily chosen reference taxon. Results We propose a framework that integrates a large target cohort that has microbiome and outcome data with a smaller external study that has paired microbiome–metabolome profiles. A high-dimensional structural equation model jointly links the microbiome, the metabolome, and the disease outcome. It allows for unmeasured confounding and groups microbes into functional categories. We address compositionality with the additive log-ratio (ALR) transformation, estimate parameters by penalized two-stage least squares, and test metabolite–disease associations with a regularized permutation test. A novel multiple-reference procedure treats each microbe in turn as the ALR reference. It combines the resulting P -values with the Cauchy combination test and classifies microbes by stability selection, which makes inference robust to the choice of reference. In simulations, the method controls the type I error rate, and its power increases with both target and external sample sizes. An application to inflammatory bowel disease, integrating the FRAN and iHMP cohorts, reveals biologically interpretable microbiome–metabolome–disease links. Availability and implementation The method is implemented in the R package MMDP, freely available at https://github.com/lei-fang-stat/MMDP .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Distilling direct effects via conditional differential gene expression analysis
item.description: Abstract Motivation Differential gene expression (DGE) analysis is foundational for interpreting RNA sequencing data, but it conflates direct biological effects with correlations propagated through gene co-expression. Across three RNA sequencing datasets (including a genome-scale perturb-seq experiment), we find that only a small fraction of differentially expressed genes have direct effects on the trait of interest, while the majority are undirected or passengers whose associations are mediated through other genes. Results To distinguish direct effect genes, we introduce conditional differential gene expression (CDGE) analysis, a framework that tests for conditional rather than marginal association between each gene and the trait of interest. Implemented via the GhostKnockoff procedure with lasso regression, CDGE delivers false discovery rate control, operates on summary statistics from existing DGE pipelines, and accommodates batch effects. The genes identified by CDGE mediate the effects of most other differentially expressed genes and show stronger enrichment for known protein–protein interactions and biological pathways than DGE-identified genes. These results suggest that the field has been systematically over-interpreting DGE outputs, and that distinguishing direct from mediated effects is essential for prioritizing genes for functional follow-up and therapeutic development. Availability and implementation To facilitate public access to knockoff-based CDGE analysis, we have developed the R package “KnockoffCDGE” as an integrated implementation, which is freely available at https://github.com/GuJQ5/KnockoffCDGE (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23241517).

item.title: Bioinformatics: ARCHER-LD: rapid long-range linkage disequilibrium calculations at biobank scale using GPU acceleration
item.description: Abstract Summary Linkage disequilibrium (LD) information from one’s own dataset is considered optimal for downstream analyses such as statistical fine-mapping. However, the computational complexity (≈N22 computations for N variants) leads most studies to use external reference panels, such as from 1000 Genomes. To capture LD across all variant pairs in biobank-scale whole-genome sequencing (WGS) datasets with hundreds of millions of variants, new computational strategies are essential. We present a novel approach that uses multi-GPU distributed computing to compute R2 for every variant pair in a dataset. On chromosome 22 (1.8 million variants) of the 30× WGS 1000 Genomes dataset, our method using eight consumer-level 12 GB GPUs (NVIDIA RTX 2080TIs) takes <10 min, while the same calculation with PLINK using a high-end 64-threaded CPU (Intel Xeon Gold 6338) takes >80 min, corresponding to a ≈8× speedup. We further demonstrate true biobank-scale performance in the Penn Medicine Biobank (57 170 samples), computing chromosome 1 LD (≈1.38 million variants) in 49 min versus 22.7 h for PLINK, a ≈28× speedup. With this method, we successfully computed on the aforementioned 30× WGS 1000 Genomes dataset (≈120 million variants and ≈2500 samples) the entire LD matrix (>1e16, or 10 quadrillion elements) in under 6 h using 512 NVIDIA 40GB A100 GPUs on the Department of Energy Argonne Leadership Computing Facility Polaris Supercomputer. We make this tool, Accelerated Rapid Computation of High-throughput Extensive Recombination and Linkage Disequilibrium (ARCHER-LD), coded in Python using CuPy, publicly available. Using this tool, researchers can leverage the full extent of their genomic data without relying on external LD reference panels and acquire more accurate, population-specific findings, particularly for groups underrepresented in existing databases. Availability and implementation ARCHER-LD is an open-source tool available on GitHub under the Apache License 2.0 at https://github.com/rachitk/ARCHER-LD . The version of record used in this manuscript is archived via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23399887 .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Revisiting batch effect correction: a structured problem formulation and novel solutions
item.description: Abstract Motivation Existing methods for batch effect removal often suffer from an ill-defined problem formulation and rely on unverified assumptions, limiting their robustness and generalizability. This study proposes a principled approach to systematically address these limitations. Results We present two novel methodologies for removing systematic batch effects: an unsupervised approach based on independent component analysis and a supervised approach using a domain adaptation technique. Both methods are grounded in rigorous mathematical principles. Our approaches outperform existing methods across multiple datasets. Availability and implementation The implementation of our methods, including all code, datasets, experimental workflows, and supplementary material, is available in Python and has been made publicly accessible on GitHub: https://github.com/shaham-lab/revisiting-batch-effect-removal .

item.title: Bioinformatics: Microenvironment awareness pragmatic analysis for generative enzyme function reasoning
item.description: Abstract Motivation Accurate enzyme function annotation is critical for interpreting rapidly expanding sequence data, yet experimental methods are costly and low-throughput, while computational approaches face two key limitations. Most existing methods are discriminative models confined to known EC labels, making it difficult to generalize to emerging enzymatic activities under cold-start conditions. Moreover, they typically treat enzymes as isolated molecular entities and overlook microenvironment factors such as optimal pH and temperature, which provide important contextual clues for functional annotation. Results This study proposes Microenvironment awareness pragmatic analysis for generative enzyme function reasoning, a generative framework that integrates microenvironment as pragmatic context into enzyme function reasoning. By fine-tuning the large language model on a newly constructed Enzyme Microenvironment Database, the model learns to infer microenvironment from sequence and then reason function within that context, generating EC labels with explicit reasoning chains. Multi-task enzyme microenvironment prediction imputes missing pH and temperature values to complete the Enzyme Microenvironment Database. On public benchmark dataset, Microenvironment Awareness Pragmatic Analysis for Generative Enzyme Function Reasoning achieves an absolute F1 improvement of 0.1068 over the state-of-the-art GraphEC model. Under cold-start conditions, the model generates reference-worthy function labels, demonstrating its practical utility for emerging enzymatic activities. Availability and implementation The source code and data of MPA-EC can be accessed at https://bliulab.net/MPA-EC , https://zenodo.org/records/22152329 and https://github.com/bliulab/MPA-EC .

item.title: Bioinformatics: TL-iGeneCombo: transfer learning for individual sample specific gene combination effect prediction and selection in cancer cells
item.description: Abstract Motivation Identifying effective gene combinations is critical for developing combinatorial cancer therapies. Synthetic lethality (SL) has been widely used to characterize genetic interactions based on cell viability, but predictive models are often limited by the availability of combinatorial double-knockout (CDKO) data for individual cancer cells. How to borrow information from CDKO experiments in other cancer cells to improve prediction in a targeted cancer cell remains an important challenge. Results We investigated the CDKO effects of paired genes using both SL as an indirect measure and gene combination effect as a direct measure. We developed TL-iGeneCombo, a transfer learning approach, to borrow data from CDKO experiments in other cancer cells for the prediction of SL and gene combination effect in a targeted cancer cell. Applying TL-iGeneCombo improved the accuracy of SL classification by 19% and increased the Spearman correlation of gene combination effect scores by 29%. Using data and models built from the first CDKO experiment in a prostate cancer cell, 22RV1, we further designed gene pairs for a second CDKO experiment in the same cell. It validated the superior prediction of gene combination effect, but not SL prediction. Availability and implementation The software is freely available at https://github.com/BirkanGokbag/TL-iGeneCombo under the GNU General Public License v.3.0.
